newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST-Bank/Portugal has room to ease rates.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bank/Portugal has room to ease rates.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal has room to ease its key repo and draining rates tomorrow on the eve of a new commercial bank reserve period, but may refrain from doing so just a week after the last cut in the repo, analysts said.
Seven dealers and economists contacted by Reuters said they thought the central bank had room to ease rates, but only two believed it would do so this week.

"It's possible nothing will happen, but it is vital to take advantage of the falling rates because, if Germany is growing more quickly than expected, probably rates have already hit a 'bottom' and then it will be more difficult to lower rates further and buck the trend," said the chief dealer of a bank.
Isabel Cabral of Lisbon broker Fincor said: "I have some doubts about this week but, either tomorrow or next month, the Bank of Portugal will have to cut its draining rate."
The Bank of Portugal's repo rate is now 7.0 percent and its draining rate is 6.80 percent.
Portugal's repo rate has eased gradually this year from 8.50 percent at the start of 1996. The central bank trimmed the repo rate by 10 basis points last week.
Analysts said the Bank of Portugal may resist rate cuts this week because of some turbulence in international foreign exchange markets and a rise in bond yields.
Monetary policy would depend on the progress of the present round of 1997 public sector wage talks, banking sources said.

The national wage deal being negotiated with civil servant unions would probably end up seeing salary rises "slightly above" 2.5 percent, Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said in a television interview on Wednesday night.
The government has so far offered 2.375 percent, the mid-point of its 2.25-2.50 inflation forecast for next year.
But unions representing over 500,000 public sector employees, whose salary deals are usually a benchmark for the private sector, are seeking at least 4.5 percent.
Fincor's Cabral said a wage agreement of up to three percent would not disrupt the objectives of the government's 1997 budget proposals now being considered by parliament.
